analysis.one_liner: Ties federal airport funding to a $15 minimum wage and benefits for airport service workers.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 97 House Democrats, never left the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and received no vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required small, medium, and large hub airports to certify that service workers — security officers, cleaners, baggage handlers, ticketing agents, food and retail workers — are paid at least $15 an hour (or the higher local or prevailing wage) with fringe benefits, as a condition of receiving federal airport grants and passenger facility charges. It would also have applied the same labor standards to unspent airport infrastructure money from the 2021 infrastructure law. Airports that refused to certify compliance would lose access to those federal funds.
analysis.who_benefits: Roughly hundreds of thousands of airport service workers who load bags, clean terminals, screen passengers' documents, and staff food courts and shops. Most are employed by contractors, not the airlines, and many earn near the minimum wage with limited benefits. The bill set a wage and benefits floor tied to federal dollars the airports already receive, and explicitly covered workers regardless of what kind of contract linked them to an employer. Travelers could also benefit from a more stable, less transient workforce.

how_it_helps.text: Requires hub airports to certify that covered service workers are paid at least the highest of $15 per hour, the Service Contract Act prevailing wage, the federal contract minimum wage, or the applicable state or local minimum wage.

Requires fringe benefits at least as high as the Service Contract Act minimum or applicable state and local law, whichever is greater, with the Labor Department issuing wage determinations for each class of covered worker within 90 days of enactment.
Covers workers regardless of any alleged contractual relationship with a contractor or subcontractor, closing the common loophole where staffing chains hide who is responsible for wages.

Conditions federal airport development grants, passenger facility charge approvals, discretionary grants, and remaining Airport Infrastructure Grants and Airport Terminal Program funds from the 2021 infrastructure law on compliance with the wage and benefits standards.

analysis.who_pays: Airport operators and the airlines, food service, retail, security, and cleaning contractors that employ airport service workers would bear higher labor costs. Some of that cost would likely be passed to travelers through concession prices or airport fees, and a small share of airports in low-wage areas might have reduced projects rather than raise wages.

drawbacks.text: Higher mandated wages and benefits raise costs for airports and their service contractors, which could be passed on to travelers through higher concession and ticket-adjacent prices.
Because the wage floor is a condition on federal grants, an airport that chose not to comply would forgo federal infrastructure money, potentially delaying terminal and runway projects.
The bill's wage determinations would have had to be issued within 90 days of enactment for every class of covered worker, a timetable that could have produced rushed or contested classifications.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — a living wage and benefits floor for some of the lowest-paid workers in aviation, funded as a condition of federal money — is large and targeted, and the bill preserved any stronger state or local wage laws rather than overriding them. The main costs are higher labor expenses for airports and contractors and the risk that a few noncompliant airports forgo federal grants. Weighing them, the gains to hundreds of thousands of low-wage workers outweigh the diffuse price effects, though the grant-leverage mechanism means airports in low-wage regions faced the sharpest adjustment.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then to its Aviation Subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Chuy Garcia introduced the bill on March 9, 2023, joined by 30 original cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure on March 9, 2023, and to the Subcommittee on Aviation on March 10, 2023.
It attracted 97 cosponsors, all of them Democrats.

The bill never advanced past subcommittee referral: the action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action for the remainder of the Congress, which ended January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Airports and the airlines and service contractors that employ airport workers are better off because the bill never moved: they avoid the higher wage and benefit costs the certification requirement would have imposed. Airport service workers gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Jesus 'Chuy' Garcia
for.role: Sponsor, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 30 original cosponsors from the Democratic caucus.

for.name: 97 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support; none of the bill's cosponsors were Republican.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee / Aviation Subcommittee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Republicans
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote in the 22 months before the Congress ended.

against.name: Chair Sam Graves
against.role: Chair, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired never scheduled the bill for consideration; it died at the subcommittee-referral stage. (Chair identity is general public knowledge, not in the provided sources.)

sides.party_line_note: All 97 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; the bill died in a Republican-chaired committee without ever reaching a recorded vote.

industries.note: Airports receiving federal grants and passenger facility charges would have had to certify wage and benefit floors for their service workforce or lose access to that federal money. Many operate concession and service contracts through low-wage staffing chains that the bill would have repriced.

industries.industry: Airlines and airline service contractors (ground handling, catering, security, cleaning)
industries.note: Airlines largely outsource baggage handling, cleaning, and passenger assistance to contractors; the bill would have required those contractors to raise pay and benefits for work done on airport property. Airlines' interest in keeping this labor cheap runs against the workers' and travelers' interest in a stable, trained workforce.

industries.industry: Airport food service and retail concession companies
industries.note: Concession workers — cooks, cashiers, servers, cleaners — were expressly covered, so concession operators would have faced the same wage and benefits floor at every hub airport taking federal funds.
